I used to have insomnia - and still do some nights. These are some of the things that worked for me:

* Brush teeth and change into pajamas at least an hour before going to bed. Some people learn to associate brushing teeth with waking up in the mornings, and feel more alert afterwards.

* Make a quick list of things to do the next day. Make sure there's a pad and pen beside the bed.

* Always have at least two alarm options - phone, watch, alarm clock etc. Some people worry about sleeping in so much that they can't sleep.

* Phase in sleep. Don't shut off the TV and expect to fall asleep right away, you can't do it. Transition into quiet. TV off at least half an hour before bed. If you read, all other lights should be off. Get a reading light dimmer, and about 15 minutes go to a lower setting. Your eyes will strain a little harder and will want to close.

* Give yourself some time after the lights are out to think about things. I like to think about snowboarding through powder or riding my bike through a forest. I don't think about my day, about work, about tomorrow, or anything that can get me riled up. That's my time.

* I don't worry about closing my eyes. If I'm relaxed, they'll close on their own.

* If I can't fall asleep I try to figure out why. Is there something I need to write down? Is there a noise I'm not used to? A light that's distracting me? Do I have to pee? Even something small, like the fact that my pajamas are twisted, will keep me up.

Like I said, these things work for me. I hope they can work for you.

Don't forget about homeowners' associations - a lot of people are encouraging younger generations to get into the condo market for their starter homes, and I don't think people realize how much homeowners' association fees are really going to cost. They often start too low and increase over time - our fees have doubled at my place in less than 10 years, partly because of a new law that requires us to account for depreciation of common assets. It's a good law, but now we're paying about 35% of our housing costs to the association for very little service - some snow clearing, landscaping, and insurance.

Edit: When I say it starts too low, I'm referring to new developments. Typically the costs are low, but increase over time to reflect the actual expenses. Whether this is a deliberate strategy to make the units more appealing to the first buyers, I have no idea.

In a certain province, community fees cover both maintenance costs and fixed costs. Previously, you didn't have to include the full cost of depreciating assets like a roof or shared spaces, but that's now part of the reason my fees have doubled since 2006. For a 1,400 square foot townhouse in a complex with about 90 other townhouses, we're paying about $3,500 a year in community fees (just under $300/month) - that covers garbage removal, snow clearing, landscaping, electricity costs for street lighting, irrigation, and the maintenance of the grounds and shared spaces - although we have had to pay surcharges for things like painting in the past because we didn't have enough saved up to cover those costs.

That's over a full month of after-tax salary for me, which is a huge chunk of money when you factor in the cost of the mortgage, ($11,000), groceries, child care, car insurance, house insurance, utilities, etc. Luckily we're a two-income family, or we wouldn't be able to afford even our modest house. We haven't saved a dime for our retirement since our child was born, and we can't afford to go away.

Even worse, our community costs seem to be increasing every year at a rate that's well above inflation, while our wages are pretty much stagnant. It's becoming a massive burden.

My advice for homeowners is to either avoid buying anywhere that has a community fee structure, or to get involved in the community management to protect your investment and prevent others with more financial resources from signing onto projects you don't need or want. Even then, there's little you can do - there's one company that does garbage removal in my area, we do get snow, insurance costs are increasing, the buildings are aging; it's not like the community management is wasting money, and they do try to get competitive bids on everything.

The problem is that the stock market, and the need to post quarterly profits, forces short-term thinking on companies that might otherwise take the long view. They need more revenues, and they need them now to keep investors happy - and ensure their own equity holdings maintain their value. However, I think an honest announcement - "the media landscape has changed drastically, and it's clear that we can't go back... this is what we're doing to move forward" - would be better received than they expect, and prevent investors from abandoning ship.

Still, a large tech company could have started in a major city like one in the Northeast, a city in Southern California, or a city in the Midwest where there's enough population density to justify the investment, but instead I think they chose a smaller city in the Midwest. If they can make a go of it in smaller markets, then I imagine cities in Canada should be relatively easy.

The answer for a city in the Pacific Northwest and a city in Ontario is the same thing that worked for a popular resort town - create an alternative housing market by leveraging the power of zoning.

In the resort town, there's an entire employee/resident housing market with rentals and for-purchase homes, townhomes, apartments, etc. To qualify, you have to live and work in the area, and prequalify for a mortgage covering that amount. You also have to sign a covenant that gives away some of the rights you would normally have.

The for-purchase units do appreciate in value, but only as much as inflation. While one city jumps up significantly, the resort town homes appreciated a more sensible rate, ensuring a reasonable return for sellers - and incentive to reinvest in the home - while ensuring the properties are still affordable for the next person. The rental units are rent controlled, with rates tied to the cost of repaying construction costs.

If you no longer work in the resort or purchase another market house, you have to sell your restricted property to the next person on the list - holding onto it is not an option under the covenant you agree to. You're also not eligible to buy in if it's not your primary residence.

The best part? Developers love it. Most of these restricted units were built in exchange for rezoning parcels of land. Imagine a parcel of land that's 10 acres but is only zoned for one home: the developer will apply to subdivide that land into smaller market lots, and will happily agree to setting aside a number of those lots to build restricted housing - and can even profit by selling it for a little above construction costs. Everybody wins - the resort town has space for employees, locals can afford to buy homes, and developers get the zoning they need to profit from their land investment. More importantly, those developers are typically local and employ local tradespeople who can also now afford to live in the area.

Some of the side benefits include great local neighborhoods for young families, high-density housing that's more cost-effective to serve, and more dependable year-round business for local businesses.

Why ignore it? I love my country - we've created one of the most stable, highest functioning nations on the planet with a standard of living that is the envy of the world. But our mistreatment, attempted gentrification, and marginalization of Indigenous peoples is a black stain.

I'm under no illusions that Indigenous peoples would have been left alone in the age of colonization - if not the British, they would have been taken over, and left in an even worse position, by the French, Americans, Spanish, Dutch, or any of the other major colonizing powers. Even the Russians might have laid claim to the western part of the country.

But when I compare our situation to other countries with Indigenous populations - like a nation in the South Pacific - we have a lot to be ashamed about. Everyone in my country should study Indigenous languages and culture instead of dismissing them as untamed savages fit for replacement by cultured Europeans. We should be renaming landmarks according to Indigenous names. Indigenous peoples should be able to leave their reserves and feel honoured, respected, reflected, and understood everywhere they go.

In the South Pacific nation, the Indigenous warrior culture is respected. They have guaranteed representation in government and land trusts, and every citizen I've ever met can speak some of the language - the traditional war dance, the Indigenous version of the national anthem, a lot of sayings and phrases, etc. When the national rugby team, one of the world's great sports dynasties, hits the pitch, they always have Indigenous representation as well. It's not perfect by a long stretch, but it's better than anything we have here.

We could and should be doing a lot more. It's not as easy as in the South Pacific nation - there are more core Indigenous languages and cultures in my country for one thing - but it's not impossible. Everybody on the West Coast should know some local Indigenous languages, Prairie dwellers should know some from the Plains tribes, residents of central regions should know some from the northern tribes, etc.

In my mind this is the only viable solution to the so-called Indigenous problem. Let Indigenous peoples feel respected and valued, and reassured that their traditions will carry on, and they will feel better leaving reserves, joining the workforce, and integrating into a country that is supposed to welcome diversity.

The problem is that Indigenous governance is a bit messy right now - some communities are doing well and like the status quo, others are suffering and want revenge and restitution, others just want an increase in funding and powers of self-government, etc. The highest court has already given Indigenous groups de facto partnership rights when it comes to resource applications, which is a good first step, but you are right - there needs to be a renegotiation of status within the country. To start with, I'd like to see Indigenous groups get guaranteed representation in government and the Senate, like they do in another country, as well as in regional legislatures - something that would be relatively easy if we could just get the electoral system changed to proportional representation.

It would also be beneficial if the changes weren't top down. Right now we negotiate with community leaders and they win concessions and funding that tends to go directly to community governance, which presumably - but not always - trickles it down to the community members. While that's necessary (even if it puts the money and resources beyond our control) I'm more concerned with taking a leg up approach with community members, and making them feel more comfortable joining in with the economy.

For example, I live in a resort area that brings in workers from around the world - Australians, South Americans, Filipinos, etc. - to work in restaurants and hotels. Meanwhile there's an Indigenous community 30 minutes in one direction with over 40% unemployment, and another community 45 minutes in the other with over 30% unemployment. I really think accommodation would empower those potential workers to join the workforce here. It would really only take them a decade before they'd be running this place in management roles, acting as role models in their communities and laying the groundwork for hiring more Indigenous individuals.

For that to happen, we would have to help out at first by subsidizing transit, making allowances for community traditions like multi-day funerals, increasing Indigenous language and cultural visibility so they feel comfortable, and giving the workers some leeway to make mistakes as they come on board. It will be tough and expensive, but at the end of the day it will be worth it.
